text:
A man who was unhoused and “unable to defend himself due to health issues” was recently beaten to death and had his prescription medication taken outside a pharmacy in New Orleans, according to authorities.
The killing of 68-year-old David Hyde led police to arrest Antonio Myles, 19, on a count of second-degree murder, with investigators alleging that they came to suspect the much younger man after he had bragged to others about fatally beating an unhoused person.
As portrayed in criminal court records summarizing the circumstances surrounding Myles’ arrest, Hyde’s killing is an extreme example of how people experiencing homelessness in the US are at heightened risk of being victimized by violence.
A 2020 US justice department study determined that about half of people experiencing homelessness report being victims of violence – a rate that for the general population is 2%. And in May, amid an affordability crisis in the US, the federal Housing and Urban Development said the most recent available point-in-time estimate calculated that nearly 700,000 people were experiencing homelessness nationwide when the count was conducted on a night in January.
New Orleans police said officers found Hyde down outside a Walgreens in the 4400 block of Claiborne Avenue, on the edge of the city’s Freret neighborhood, at about 6.55am on 8 November “with severe contusions to his face”. He was near numerous prescription medication bottles and pronounced dead at the scene from what investigators ascertained to be kicks to the head, as evident from the shoe prints left on Hyde’s face, police wrote in sworn count documents.
Investigators later secured video from a store surveillance camera that showed Hyde sitting near the pharmacy’s front entrance when his attacker took his backpack, dumped its contents on the ground and picked some of those items up prior to the beating. While the deadly violence evidently happened out of the camera’s view, the man who approached Hyde at one point used his shirt to wipe his shoes and then left the scene.
Police alleged they received a call a day later reporting that Myles had been heard “bragging to unknown subjects that he was responsible for beating a homeless man to death”. Myles was soon interviewed by police, but they released him pending further investigation, according to the sworn statement summarizing the case.
Then, on 10 November, police investigating Hyde’s killing released video from a surveillance camera overlooking a parking lot which depicted a figure described as a “suspect wanted in connection with a brutal beating that left a disabled man dead”.
“The victim … was unable to defend himself due to health issues,” police said in a statement accompanying the video, without elaborating. Police asked anyone who recognized the figure to call them.
An unidentified “known subject” then told police the person in the video was Myles. That person also reportedly alleged Myles was wearing a beanie-style cap at the time of Hyde’s beating. Investigators said they later recovered surveillance footage which established Myles was wearing a beanie-style cap when Hyde was killed.
Furthermore, police said that a detective interviewed an unidentified but known subject who reported that Myles had called hours after Hyde was discovered dead. The sworn police statement accused Myles of telling that person “he loved them, and that he killed a homeless man, and continued to kick him after he was already dead”.
“The known subject also advised … that Mr Myles advised a known subject that he killed the homeless man and took his prescription medication that was inside his backpack,” the sworn police statement said. Police also said that person knew Myles well and identified him as being on the video released to the public.
According to the police statement, investigators believed that information was true because “no specific details of the investigation were released to the media”.
“Only a person who was there when the homicide occurred would know that the victim was kicked to his head repeatedly, and that the victim was in possession of prescription medicine inside of a backpack,” said the police statement, which was not available to the news media until Monday.
A New Orleans criminal court magistrate commissioner gave police permission to arrest Myles on a count of murder on Friday. He soon turned himself over to police and was jailed – and no bond was immediately set for him, court records show.
Myles’ arrest in Hyde’s killing came after he pleaded guilty to a charge of simple battery on 11 August in an unrelated case and was sentenced to about a month in jail, according to court records. He would receive mandatory life imprisonment if eventually convicted of second-degree murder.
